why_this_tool: OpenTelemetry is the vendor-neutral standard that defines logs, metrics, traces, context propagation and the GenAI span conventions in one place, so what you practise here carries over to whichever backend a customer already runs.
alternatives: Prometheus with Grafana covers metrics and dashboards only; Jaeger stores and displays traces but does not instrument code; Datadog is a paid hosted suite with its own agent; Langfuse, LangSmith and Arize Phoenix are LLM-focused trace and evaluation tools that view model calls and prompts rather than the whole system.

setup.do: Read the overview of the main OpenTelemetry components so you know what the API, SDK, OTLP and the Collector each do before installing anything.
setup.done_when: You can say in one sentence each what the API, the SDK, OTLP and the Collector are responsible for.
setup.why: Every later step names one of these parts. Knowing which piece creates telemetry and which piece ships it stops you from debugging the wrong layer.

steps.why: Seeing the metric arrive proves the whole export path works. It also shows you how instrument names appear on the backend side.

steps.do: Create a Grafana dashboard with one panel for request rate and one for latency from the sample application.
steps.done_when: The dashboard shows two panels with live data from the running application.

source.title: Export to Prometheus and Grafana | OpenTelemetry

steps.why: A dashboard is where the metrics signal becomes something an on-call person reads. Building one makes you choose which numbers matter.

steps.do: Write one service level indicator and one service level objective for the sample application, and note which metric would trigger an alert when the objective is at risk.
steps.done_when: You have a written indicator, an objective with a target value, and one named alert condition tied to a metric on your dashboard.
steps.why: Alerts should fire on user-visible reliability, not on every noisy number. The primer explains how indicators and objectives connect metrics to that decision.

steps.do: Read the logs section of the primer and compare what a log line, a metric sample and a span each tell you about the same request.
steps.done_when: You can state for one failing request which signal detects it, which locates it and which explains it.
steps.why: The three signals answer different questions. Knowing which one to reach for is the basis for deciding what to alert on and what to keep only for investigation.

steps.do: Create a parent span with two child spans in the sample application, add attributes and a span event, set an error status on one child, and export them to the console.
steps.done_when: The console output shows three spans sharing one trace id, with parent ids, your attributes and one error status.
steps.why: Spans, attributes, events and status are the core object model of tracing. Agent traces later in this path are built from exactly these parts.

steps.do: Run a second small service, call it from the first over HTTP, and configure context propagation so both services write spans into the same trace.
steps.done_when: Spans from both services show the same trace id and the second service's span lists the first service's span as its parent.
steps.why: Distributed tracing only works when the trace context crosses the process boundary. Doing it by hand once shows what the propagation headers carry.

steps.do: Write an agent trace by hand: one span for the agent task, child spans for a model call and a tool execution, with names and attributes taken from the generative AI semantic conventions. Use a stubbed model response so no paid API is needed.
steps.done_when: The exported trace shows an agent span with model and tool child spans carrying convention-named attributes for the model and token usage.
steps.why: Shared attribute names for model, token counts and tool names are what let any backend explain cost and latency per task. A stub keeps the exercise on your laptop.

steps.do: Configure a local Collector pipeline that deletes or redacts the attributes holding prompt and completion text before the spans are exported.
steps.done_when: Spans leaving the Collector no longer contain the prompt text attribute while token counts and model name remain.
steps.why: Prompt content often contains personal or confidential data and should not reach a shared backend by default. Removing it in the pipeline protects every service at once.

steps.do: Configure sampling in the local Collector so that only a fraction of successful agent traces is kept while traces with errors are always kept.
steps.done_when: After many requests the backend holds all error traces and visibly fewer successful ones than were sent.
steps.why: Agent traces are large and telemetry volume drives cost. Sampling is the main control for keeping the useful traces and dropping the routine ones.

steps.do: Write an alert rule for your service level objective and a matching runbook entry, modelled on the published alert runbooks, and keep both in version control next to the application.
steps.done_when: The repository contains one alert rule file and one runbook entry stating meaning, impact, diagnosis and mitigation.
steps.why: An alert without a runbook leaves the responder guessing. Storing rules and runbooks as files makes the alerting setup reproducible on any machine.

steps.do: Start Jaeger locally, point the trace exporter at it over OTLP, and open the agent trace from the earlier step in the Jaeger interface.
steps.done_when: Jaeger shows the agent trace as a timeline with the model call and tool spans nested under the agent span across both services.
steps.why: A trace backend turns span output into a timeline you can search by service and duration. This is how you explain a slow or expensive agent task to a customer.

steps.do: Configure the application for the production usage guidance: a named service resource, an OTLP endpoint taken from configuration instead of code, and export through the Collector with redaction and sampling in place.
steps.done_when: Changing only configuration switches the export target, and traces in Jaeger arrive under your service name with prompt content removed.
steps.why: Production differs from the demo in where the endpoint lives, how the service is identified and what is filtered before storage. Applying the guidance last ties every earlier step into one deployable setup.
